lessons.title: Stages of Potato Growth and Development
lessons.body: Potato growth has five clear stages. Knowing them helps you act at the right time. Stage 1 is sprouting: from planting to emergence, which takes 10â20 days depending on soil temperature. You'll see small shoots break the soil. Stage 2 is vegetative growth: leaves and stems grow fast, and the plant builds its canopy. This lasts 30â45 days. Stage 3 is tuber initiation: tiny tubers form at the tips of underground stems (stolons). This happens when the plant has 6â8 leaves and days are warm but nights cool. Stage 4 is tuber bulking: tubers swell and fill with starch. This is the longest stage, 45â60 days. Stage 5 is maturity: vines yellow and die, skins set, and tubers are ready. In Africa, many farmers grow two crops a year. If you plant in March, emergence by early April, tuber initiation by mid-May, bulking through JuneâJuly, and harvest in August. For a second crop, plant in August, harvest in December. Walk your field twice a week. Count days from planting. At stage 3, avoid heavy nitrogenâit delays tubers. At stage 4, keep soil moist; drought now cuts yield. At stage 5, stop watering 2 weeks before harvest to toughen skins. Use a notebook to record dates for each stage. Compare with your neighbours. If your crop is late, check for disease or poor soil. Recognising stages prevents mistakes like fertilising too late or harvesting too early. With practice, you'll know each stage by looking at leaf colour and plant height.

lessons.title: Scouting for Plant Health and Stress
lessons.body: Scouting means walking your field regularly to spot problems early. Do it at least twice a week, in the morning when pests are active. Walk in a zigzag pattern, not just along edges. Check 10 random spots per hectare. Look at leaves, stems, and soil. Common pests in Africa: aphids (small green or black insects on leaf undersides), potato tuber moth (larvae bore into leaves and tubers), and cutworms (cut seedlings at soil level). Diseases: late blight (dark water-soaked spots with white mould on leaf edges), early blight (brown spots with rings), and bacterial wilt (plants wilt suddenly, tubers rot). Stress signs: yellowing leaves (nitrogen shortage), purple leaf edges (phosphorus shortage), curled leaves (heat or drought stress), and small leaves (waterlogging). Use a hand lens (10x) to see aphids and mite eggs. Carry a notebook and record: date, location, pest/disease, severity (1â5 scale). For aphids, if you find 5â10 per leaf, spray neem oil (5 ml per litre of water) or insecticidal soap. For late blight, remove infected plants and spray copper-based fungicide (e.g., copper oxychloride at 3 g per litre). For cutworms, handpick at dusk or apply wood ash around stems. Always check soil moisture: dig 10 cm deep. If dry, irrigate. If waterlogged, improve drainage. Scouting saves moneyâyou treat only when needed. Keep records to see patterns. Share findings with other farmers. Early action stops small problems from becoming total loss.

lessons.title: Using Growing Degree Days for Crop Management
lessons.body: Growing Degree Days (GDD) measure heat accumulation. Potatoes need a certain GDD to reach each stage. To calculate daily GDD: add daily maximum and minimum temperatures, divide by 2, then subtract the base temperature. For potatoes, base temperature is 7Â°C. Example: max 25Â°C, min 15Â°C. Average = (25+15)/2 = 20. GDD = 20 - 7 = 13. If you sum daily GDD from planting, you can predict stages. Typical GDD requirements: emergence at 150â200 GDD, tuber initiation at 300â400 GDD, start of bulking at 500â600 GDD, maturity at 1200â1500 GDD. In warm African areas, you may accumulate 15â20 GDD per day. So tuber initiation could occur 20â25 days after planting. In cooler highlands, only 8â10 GDD per day, so it takes 35â40 days. Use a simple max-min thermometer (cost $5â10) in your field. Record daily max and min at 8 AM. Calculate GDD each day and add to a running total. When you reach 300 GDD, start checking for tuber initiationâdig up one plant gently. When you reach 500 GDD, ensure consistent moisture for bulking. If GDD is behind schedule, your crop may be delayed by cold or stress. If ahead, harvest earlier. GDD helps you time fertiliser, irrigation, and harvest. It works anywhere, but you need local temperature data. Many African meteorological services provide free online GDD calculators. Ask your extension officer for help. Keep a GDD log in your notebook. This turns farming into a predictable plan.

lessons.title: Canopy Management and Light Interception
lessons.body: The canopy is the leaves and stems above ground. A healthy canopy captures sunlight to make starch for tubers. Aim for a full canopy that covers the soil by 40â50 days after planting. If plants are too close, they compete for light and air, increasing disease. If too far apart, you waste land. Recommended spacing: 75 cm between rows and 30 cm between plants for medium varieties. That gives about 44,000 plants per hectare. For small farms, use 60 cm x 25 cm. To manage canopy, you may need to prune excess leaves if they shade tubers too much. But do not remove more than 10% of leaves. In Africa, many farmers intercrop potatoes with beans or maize. This can reduce potato canopy. If intercropping, plant potatoes first, then beans after 2 weeks. Light interception is how much sunlight the canopy captures. A good canopy intercepts 90% of light. You can measure this with a simple light meter (cost $20â30) or a smartphone app. Take readings above and below the canopy at noon. If below is more than 20% of above, your canopy is too sparse. To improve, apply nitrogen fertiliser (e.g., urea at 50 kg per hectare) but only before tuber initiation. After tuber initiation, extra nitrogen makes leaves grow instead of tubers. Also, ensure adequate waterâdry soil reduces leaf expansion. Watch for lodging (stems falling over). If lodging occurs, reduce nitrogen and avoid overwatering. A well-managed canopy means more sunlight converted to tuber yield. Walk your field weekly and estimate ground cover. If less than 80% covered by 50 days, you may need to adjust practices next season.

lessons.title: Tuber Initiation and Bulking Monitoring
lessons.body: Tuber initiation is when stolons (underground stems) swell at the tips to form tiny tubers. This happens around 30â40 days after planting, depending on temperature. You can check by gently digging up one plant every 3 days. Look for small tubers the size of a pea. Once you see them, stop applying nitrogen. Nitrogen now will grow leaves, not tubers. Instead, ensure phosphorus and potassium are available. A good fertiliser at this stage: NPK 0-10-20 or similar, applied at 200 kg per hectare. Bulking is when tubers grow rapidly in size and weight. It lasts 45â60 days. During bulking, the crop needs consistent moisture. Aim for soil moisture at 60â70% field capacity. If you can squeeze a handful of soil and it holds shape without dripping, it's right. Drought during bulking can cut yield by 50%. Irrigate if rainfall is less than 25 mm per week. But avoid waterloggingâit causes rot. Monitor tuber size by digging up a plant every 10 days. At the start of bulking, tubers are marble-sized. After 30 days, they should be hen-egg sized. After 60 days, they reach full size. Record average tuber weight. If tubers are small and numerous, you may have too many plants or low potassium. If few and large, you may have too much spacing. Also check for pests: tuber moth larvae leave holes. Use pheromone traps (one per hectare) to monitor moths. If you find more than 10 moths per trap per week, spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt). Harvest when vines die and skins don't rub off. Monitoring ensures you harvest at peak yield and quality.

lessons.title: Record Keeping and Data Collection
lessons.body: Record keeping turns your farm into a learning business. Without records, you repeat mistakes. Start with a simple notebook and pen. Or use a smartphone app like FarmBook or Excel. Record these for each plot: planting date, variety, seed rate, fertiliser type and amount, irrigation dates and amounts, pesticide applications, scouting notes, GDD totals, and harvest date. Also record costs and yields. For example: Plot A, 0.5 hectare, planted 15 March, variety Shangi, 500 kg seed, 100 kg DAP at planting, 50 kg urea at 30 days, irrigated 20 mm on 1 April, scouted 10 times, found aphids on 5 April, sprayed neem oil, harvested 20 July, yield 8 tonnes. That's 16 tonnes per hectare. Compare with Plot B where you did nothing. You'll see what works. Use a simple form with columns: Date, Activity, Details, Cost, Notes. At the end of the season, calculate profit: total income minus total costs. Also record weather: daily rainfall (use a rain gauge, $10) and max/min temperatures. This helps calculate GDD. Take photos of pests and diseases for future reference. Share records with your extension officer or farmer group. They can help you analyse. Many African farmers who keep records increase yields by 20â30% within two seasons. Start smallârecord only planting, fertiliser, and harvest. Then add more. Keep records for at least 3 years to see patterns. Store them in a dry place. Use a pencil if ink runs. Digital records are easy to back up. Your records are your best tool for better farming.

quiz.q: How many main stages of potato growth are there?
quiz.explanation: Potato growth has five stages: sprouting, vegetative, tuber initiation, bulking, and maturity.

quiz.q: What happens during tuber initiation?
options: B) Tiny tubers form at stolon tips
quiz.explanation: Tuber initiation is when stolon tips swell to form small tubers.

quiz.q: Which stage is the longest in potato growth?
quiz.explanation: Tuber bulking lasts 45â60 days, longer than other stages.

quiz.q: What should you avoid during tuber initiation?
quiz.explanation: Heavy nitrogen at tuber initiation delays tuber formation and promotes leaf growth.

quiz.q: When should you stop watering before harvest?
quiz.explanation: Stop watering 2 weeks before harvest to toughen skins and prevent rot.

quiz.q: How often should you scout your potato field?
quiz.explanation: Scouting twice a week helps spot pests and diseases early.

quiz.q: What is a sign of aphid infestation?
options: B) Small green or black insects on leaf undersides
quiz.explanation: Aphids are small green or black insects that cluster on leaf undersides.

quiz.q: Which disease causes dark water-soaked spots with white mould?
quiz.explanation: Late blight causes dark water-soaked spots and white mould on leaf edges.

quiz.q: What is a simple treatment for cutworms?
options: B) Apply wood ash around stems
quiz.explanation: Wood ash around stems repels or kills cutworms.

quiz.q: What does yellowing of leaves often indicate?
quiz.explanation: Yellowing leaves are a common sign of nitrogen deficiency.

quiz.q: What is the base temperature for calculating GDD for potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Potatoes have a base temperature of 7Â°C for GDD calculations.

quiz.q: How do you calculate daily GDD?
quiz.explanation: GDD = (daily max + daily min)/2 - base temperature (7Â°C).

quiz.q: About how many GDD are needed for tuber initiation?
quiz.explanation: Tuber initiation typically occurs at 300â400 GDD.

quiz.q: What tool do you need to calculate GDD?
quiz.explanation: A max-min thermometer records daily high and low temperatures needed for GDD.

quiz.q: If you accumulate 15 GDD per day, when will tuber initiation occur?
quiz.explanation: 300â400 GDD divided by 15 GDD/day gives about 20â25 days.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for medium potato varieties?
quiz.explanation: 75 cm between rows and 30 cm between plants is standard for medium varieties.

quiz.q: What percentage of light should a good canopy intercept?
quiz.explanation: A healthy canopy intercepts about 90% of sunlight.

quiz.q: When should you apply nitrogen fertiliser to avoid reducing tuber yield?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen before tuber initiation supports canopy; after, it delays tubers.

quiz.q: What is lodging in potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Lodging is when stems fall over, often due to excess nitrogen or wind.

quiz.q: How can you measure light interception simply?
options: B) Use a light meter or smartphone app
quiz.explanation: A light meter or smartphone app measures light above and below canopy.

quiz.q: What size are tubers at the start of bulking?
quiz.explanation: At the start of bulking, tubers are about marble-sized.

quiz.q: What fertiliser ratio is good for tuber bulking?
quiz.explanation: Low nitrogen, high phosphorus and potassium (e.g., 0-10-20) supports bulking.

quiz.q: What is ideal soil moisture during bulking?
quiz.explanation: 60â70% field capacity keeps soil moist but not waterlogged.

quiz.q: How often should you check tuber size during bulking?
quiz.explanation: Dig up a plant every 10 days to monitor tuber growth.

quiz.q: What pest leaves holes in tubers?
quiz.explanation: Potato tuber moth larvae bore into tubers, leaving holes.

quiz.q: What is a simple record keeping tool for farmers?
quiz.explanation: A notebook and pen is the simplest and most reliable record keeping tool.

quiz.q: Why should you record costs and yields?
quiz.explanation: Recording costs and yields helps calculate profit and improve decisions.

quiz.q: What weather data is useful for GDD calculation?
quiz.explanation: Daily max and min temperatures are needed to calculate GDD.

quiz.q: How often should you record farm activities?
options: B) At the end of season
quiz.explanation: Recording activities as they happen ensures accuracy and completeness.

quiz.q: What can happen if you keep good records for 3 years?
options: A) You see patterns and improve yields
quiz.explanation: Long-term records reveal patterns that help you make better farming decisions.
